chapter: Piron, Clarence Williams and the ODJB repertoire
title: Piron's 1915 band, the ODJB's silent films and war work, and Clarence Williams's arrival
summary: La Rocca adds that Piron played string-based ragtime in 1915, lists the ODJB's films, society dates and wartime entertaining, and says Piron sent Clarence Williams to him in New York in 1923, arguing Black players followed the ODJB.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Well you mentioned Pierron's band and what type of music they play. I forgot to mention it was in the year about 1915. I think Pierron then used mostly string instruments. And he played regular conventional ragtime like I had right on records that was of that date of error. There's some things I'd like to tell you that I may have forgotten to mention. We played for two silent movies. One of them is in the Good For Nothing by Carlisle Blackwell. He was the leading man. And her shot was Charlie Chapman. This would be the same shot as these pitchers were taken at Rice Weber's Restaurant in the 400 Club in 1970. And many other fairs for the Goulds. That's the Jay Gould family. Balls, political parties, theaters and concerts. Entertained over a million soldiers and Marines during the World War I. Sold Liberty bonds. Ballyhoed in the streets of New York City. Also at several stores in New York City. Had passes to all the forts for entertainments of the soldiers. And also entertain soldiers in different hospitals. Now, we get back to Pierron. Pierron is the man who instrumentally was mostly responsible for having this Clarence Williams come to New York. Clarence Williams came to the hotel where I live with a letter of introduction by Mr. Pierron, who I had corresponded with. Because I had already made Brown Skin famous and was published by Will Rossinger. You'll find cards to that effect in the Tulane repository. We'll prove to you that we didn't discriminate against the colored man. As been said by Marshall Steins and many others. In fact, we helped our colored brethren. You'll see here on one of these first tunes of Clarence Williams. They have My Pillar and Me by Tim Brown, Chris Smith and Clarence Williams. Clarence Williams Publishing Company, 1547 Broadway, New York City. On that, he's got a jazz tune. Now, he had never used this word before. I'm that positive that I don't have many years of my life to go. This was in 1923 that he came to New York. Before that, he was in Chicago. He was a talent scout for the Columbia where he and his wife, Eva Taylor, made recordings for Columbia. Now, if this music as they say existed and this Negro was one of the principal men of composing music, it certainly would have showed before 23, 24 and 25 that these other Negroes came up. And when they did come up, they were imitating the original Dixon and Jazz Band. Because I can show you the idioms eight years before these Negroes ever put it down on racks that they were used by the original Dixon and Jazz Band. Now, would you care to read this letter of P. Ron's? This is August 13, 1922.
